From chemistry to biology on the early Earth.
Which came first: genes or metabolism?
a self-sustaining chemical system capable of Darwinian evolution
It needs metabolism (it runs its own chemistry) and genes (it can evolve).
Fire grows & uses energy; crystals grow & organize. Neither evolves, so neither is alive.
Viruses evolve but can't copy themselves without a host cell. Alive?
Which came first, genes or metabolism?
LUCA, the last common ancestor of all life, may date to here (2024 study)
carbon in a zircon crystal 'looks' like life's carbon
carbon isotopes & possible stromatolites in Greenland
Big idea: life showed up early, within about a billion years of Earth forming.
Stanley Miller & Harold Urey spark a model early atmosphere
amino acids found when Miller's saved vials were re-tested (2008)
Methane, ammonia, hydrogen, water & sparks made amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.
Early Earth's air may not have been this rich in methane & ammonia.
It made life's building blocks without life. It did not make life.
Aldehyde + ammonia + cyanide make amino acids with no life needed. It makes many kinds, in left- & right-handed forms.
Murchison meteorite: more than 90 kinds of amino acids named. Bennu (2025): 14 of life's 20 amino acids & all 5 nucleobases.
Life itself, not just ingredients, rode to Earth on rocks from another world.
Two leading ideas for how chemistry became biology.
• RNA can copy itself & speed up reactions (ribozymes)
• mineral surfaces may help short RNA pieces grow longer
• iron-sulfur minerals at hot vents drive the first chemistry
• iron-sulfur clusters still sit inside many enzymes today
Life needs energy, a way to concentrate ingredients & a safe place to build.
Carbon is made in ordinary stars when 3 helium nuclei fuse (the triple-alpha process).
Stars spread that carbon by stellar winds (red giants) and by supernovae.
Most elements heavier than iron come from supernovae & neutron-star collisions.
Could a planet around a first-generation star host life like ours? Probably not: too few heavy elements.
IS THE UNIVERSE TUNED FOR LIFE?
Small changes to some forces would change how stars make carbon.
• We can only find ourselves in a universe that allows observers.
• So it is no surprise ours allows life.
• The universe MUST produce life to observe it.
• Some cite the double-slit experiment & Schrodinger's cat, but those don't need a human observer.

store information, copy itself & speed up reactions
Life at the extremes, and the best places beyond Earth.
If life can live there on Earth, could it live there out there?
These tiny animals survived 10 days exposed to open space in 2007 (FOTON-M3).
The microbe Methanopyrus kandleri grew at 122 °C under high pressure (Deck 20 link).
Deep-sea vent communities, found in 1977, run on chemical energy, not sunlight.
Our Sun is a G star: a middle-of-the-road yellow-white star.
has what life as we know it needs: liquid water, energy & ingredients
EUROPA: AN OCEAN UNDER THE ICE
Jupiter's icy moon, a bit smaller than our Moon
Under an ice shell about 15 to 25 km thick: a salty ocean 60 to 150 km deep, about twice Earth's ocean water.
Tidal flexing by Jupiter heats the inside & keeps the ocean liquid.
Its thin oxygen 'air' comes from radiation splitting surface ice, not from life.
Life in cracks in the ice, under the ice, or at seafloor vents?
Rain, rivers & seas of liquid methane & ethane at about minus 179 °C, under air thicker than Earth's.
Water is frozen as hard as rock. Life would need a new chemistry, with liquid methane instead of water.
Methane life might 'eat' hydrogen & acetylene. Cassini data (2010) hint hydrogen vanishes near the surface.
Nature paper calls the Cheyava Falls spots a potential biosignature
Perseverance drilled the 'Sapphire Canyon' sample from this rock in July 2024.
Its spots hold vivianite & greigite, minerals that microbes on Earth help make.
Non-living chemistry can make these minerals too.
Did life make them on ancient Mars?
• soil 'breathed out' gas when fed nutrients
• but almost no organic carbon was found

• a Mars rock found in Antarctica
• tiny shapes that looked like fossils
• non-living chemistry can make similar shapes & organics

Microbes on another world have a right to be left alone.
Terraform Mars, even if it turns out to have microbes.

Send messages to aliens, like Arecibo in 1974, not just listen.

Listening, looking & asking: where is everybody?
If they are out there, why haven't we heard them?
Technosignature = a sign of technology, not just of life.
if life is common, why have we found no sign of anyone else?
Rare Earth: Earth needed many lucky conditions, so we may be alone
Too far or too young: signals haven't reached us; we've searched very little
Great Filter: some step stops most civilizations, maybe one ahead of us
Zoo hypothesis: they see us but choose to stay hidden

every non-living way to make it
